question: What are the income-tax slabs under the new regime?
answer: Under the new regime (section 115BAC, the default) the slabs for FY 2025-26 / FY 2026-27 are: up to ₹4 lakh nil; ₹4–8 lakh 5%; ₹8–12 lakh 10%; ₹12–16 lakh 15%; ₹16–20 lakh 20%; ₹20–24 lakh 25%; above ₹24 lakh 30%. Add 4% health and education cess on the tax. Salaried people also get a ₹75,000 standard deduction, and the section 87A rebate (up to ₹60,000) makes the tax zero when taxable income is ₹12 lakh or less.
source: Finance Act 2025 slabs; incometax.gov.in tax-slab page (carried into FY 2026-27 per app finance_rules.yaml)

question: What are the old-regime income-tax slabs?
answer: Old regime (for individuals below 60): up to ₹2.5 lakh nil; ₹2.5–5 lakh 5%; ₹5–10 lakh 20%; above ₹10 lakh 30%, plus 4% cess. The 87A rebate of up to ₹12,500 applies if taxable income is ₹5 lakh or less, and the standard deduction for salaried people is ₹50,000. Its advantage is that deductions like 80C, 80D, HRA and home-loan interest still apply.
source: Income-tax Act s.115BAC vs normal rates; incometax.gov.in

question: Is the new tax regime the default?
answer: Yes. Since FY 2023-24 the new regime is the default; you opt for the old regime when you file (salaried people can switch every year, people with business income can switch back only once). Your employer deducts TDS as per the new regime unless you declare otherwise.

question: I earn 12 LPA, which tax regime is better?
answer: Almost certainly the new regime. On a ₹12 lakh salary the new regime gives a ₹75,000 standard deduction, so taxable income is ₹11.25 lakh; the slab tax is ₹52,500 but the section 87A rebate wipes it out, so you pay ₹0. In the old regime, even with ₹1.5 lakh of 80C and the ₹50,000 standard deduction, taxable income is ₹10 lakh and tax is ₹1,12,500 + 4% cess = ₹1,17,000. You would need enormous deductions (HRA plus home-loan interest plus 80C) for the old regime to win.
source: Computed from Finance Act 2025 slabs with the app's income_tax_estimate tool

question: How much tax on a 15 lakh salary in the new regime?
answer: Taxable income = ₹15,00,000 − ₹75,000 standard deduction = ₹14,25,000. Slab tax: ₹4–8 lakh at 5% = ₹20,000; ₹8–12 lakh at 10% = ₹40,000; ₹12–14.25 lakh at 15% = ₹33,750. Total ₹93,750, plus 4% cess ₹3,750 = ₹97,500 for the year (about ₹8,125 a month). No 87A rebate because taxable income exceeds ₹12 lakh.

question: At 15 LPA, how much deduction do I need for the old regime to beat the new one?
answer: New-regime tax on ₹15 lakh is ₹97,500. In the old regime the tax equals that when taxable income is about ₹9.06 lakh, so you need roughly ₹5.9 lakh of total deductions (including the ₹50,000 standard deduction) — for example HRA of ₹2 lakh, 80C ₹1.5 lakh, home-loan interest ₹2 lakh. With only 80C + 80D + standard deduction (about ₹2.25 lakh) the old-regime tax is ₹1.95 lakh, so the new regime wins.
source: Break-even computed from both slab tables (Finance Act 2025)

question: Tax on 20 lakh salary, new regime?
answer: Taxable income ₹19,25,000 after the ₹75,000 standard deduction. Tax: 5% on ₹4 lakh = ₹20,000; 10% on ₹4 lakh = ₹40,000; 15% on ₹4 lakh = ₹60,000; 20% on ₹3.25 lakh = ₹65,000. Total ₹1,85,000 + 4% cess ₹7,400 = ₹1,92,400 a year.

question: Tax on 24 lakh salary under the new regime?
Do I pay zero tax on 12.75 lakh salary?
answer: Yes, in the new regime. ₹12.75 lakh minus the ₹75,000 standard deduction leaves ₹12 lakh taxable; the slab tax of ₹60,000 is fully covered by the section 87A rebate (max ₹60,000), so the tax is nil. This is why '₹12.75 lakh tax-free' was the Budget 2025 headline for salaried people.
source: Finance Act 2025, s.87A rebate ₹60,000 up to ₹12 lakh taxable income

question: I earn 13 lakh — do I lose the whole rebate?
answer: No, marginal relief protects you. Taxable income is ₹12.25 lakh (after the ₹75,000 standard deduction); normal slab tax would be ₹63,750, but the law caps the tax at the income above ₹12 lakh, i.e. ₹25,000, plus 4% cess = ₹26,000. Marginal relief fades out around ₹12.75 lakh of taxable income, after which the full slab tax applies.

question: What is the standard deduction?
answer: A flat deduction from salary or pension income that needs no bills: ₹75,000 in the new regime (raised from ₹50,000 by Budget 2024) and ₹50,000 in the old regime. It is applied automatically by your employer when computing TDS.

question: Which deductions are still allowed in the new regime?
answer: Very few: the ₹75,000 standard deduction, the employer's NPS contribution under 80CCD(2) (up to 14% of basic + DA), the employer's EPF share, interest on a home loan for a let-out property (set off against rent), family-pension deduction, and deductions for Agniveer contributions. 80C, 80D, HRA, LTA and 24(b) on a self-occupied house are not available.

question: Can I switch between old and new regime every year?
answer: Salaried individuals (no business income) can choose either regime each year when filing the return. If you have business or professional income you can opt out of the new regime once (Form 10-IEA) and switch back only once in your lifetime.

question: How is surcharge applied on income tax?
answer: Surcharge is a tax on the tax for high incomes: 10% if total income exceeds ₹50 lakh, 15% above ₹1 crore, 25% above ₹2 crore, and 37% above ₹5 crore in the old regime (capped at 25% in the new regime). The 4% cess is then charged on tax plus surcharge. Marginal relief ensures the extra tax never exceeds the income above the threshold.
source: Finance Act surcharge schedule; s.115BAC caps surcharge at 25%

question: What is the 4% cess on income tax?
answer: The Health and Education Cess is 4% charged on your income tax (plus surcharge, if any). For example, a slab tax of ₹93,750 attracts cess of ₹3,750, so the final liability is ₹97,500.

question: What is taxable income vs gross income?
answer: Gross total income is everything you earned in the year — salary, house property, capital gains, business income, other sources. Taxable income is what remains after exemptions (like HRA) and deductions (standard deduction, 80C, 80D in the old regime). Slabs apply to taxable income, not gross.

question: How is a senior citizen taxed in the old regime?
answer: For residents aged 60–79 the old-regime basic exemption is ₹3 lakh (₹5 lakh for 80 and above); the remaining slabs are the same (5% up to ₹5 lakh, 20% to ₹10 lakh, 30% above). Seniors also get 80TTB (₹50,000 on deposit interest) and a higher 80D limit of ₹50,000. In the new regime the slabs are the same for everyone.
source: Finance Act rate schedule for senior / super-senior citizens

question: What is section 87A rebate?
answer: A rebate that cancels the tax for low and middle incomes. New regime: taxable income up to ₹12 lakh gets a rebate of up to ₹60,000 (so tax is nil), with marginal relief just above ₹12 lakh. Old regime: taxable income up to ₹5 lakh gets up to ₹12,500. The rebate does not cover special-rate income such as capital gains on listed shares.

question: Is income from a side freelance gig taxed differently from salary?
answer: It is taxed at the same slab rates but reported under 'profits and gains of business or profession'. You can deduct genuine expenses (laptop depreciation, internet, software) or use presumptive taxation under 44ADA (declare 50% of receipts as income, no books needed, receipts up to ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh if cash receipts are ≤ 5%). Having business income means you file ITR-3 or ITR-4, not ITR-1.

question: What is advance tax and when is it due?
answer: If your total tax after TDS exceeds ₹10,000 in a year you must pay it in instalments: 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December and 100% by 15 March. Missing instalments costs 1% a month interest under sections 234B and 234C. Resident senior citizens without business income are exempt. Presumptive-scheme taxpayers can pay it all by 15 March.

question: What is Form 16?
answer: Form 16 is the TDS certificate your employer must give you by 15 June for the previous financial year. Part A shows tax deducted and deposited quarter by quarter; Part B shows the salary break-up, exemptions, deductions and the tax computation. It is the main document for filing ITR-1, and it must match Form 26AS / AIS.

question: What are Form 26AS and AIS?
answer: Form 26AS is your annual tax statement: TDS/TCS deducted, advance tax and self-assessment tax paid, and refunds. The Annual Information Statement (AIS) is broader — it also lists interest, dividends, share and mutual-fund transactions, rent and high-value purchases reported by third parties. Reconcile both with your return before filing; you can give feedback on wrong AIS entries on the e-filing portal.

question: How is HRA exemption calculated?
answer: In the old regime the exempt HRA is the least of: (1) actual HRA received, (2) rent paid minus 10% of salary (basic + DA), (3) 50% of salary in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata or Chennai, else 40%. Example: basic ₹50,000/month, HRA ₹20,000/month, rent ₹18,000/month in Bengaluru → (1) ₹2.4 lakh, (2) ₹2.16 lakh − ₹0.6 lakh = ₹1.56 lakh, (3) ₹2.4 lakh; exempt HRA = ₹1.56 lakh a year. Rent above ₹1 lakh a year needs the landlord's PAN.

question: Can I claim HRA if I live with my parents?
answer: Yes, if you genuinely pay rent to them: transfer the rent to their bank account, keep a rent agreement and receipts, and they must show it as rental income in their return (they can claim the 30% standard deduction on it). You cannot claim HRA for a house you own yourself.

question: What is section 24(b)?
answer: Deduction for interest on a home loan. For a self-occupied house you can deduct up to ₹2 lakh of interest a year (old regime only); for a let-out property the full interest is deductible against rent, with the overall house-property loss set-off capped at ₹2 lakh a year. Pre-construction interest is claimed in five equal instalments after possession.

question: What is section 80E?
answer: Deduction (old regime) for the interest paid on an education loan for yourself, spouse, children or a student you are legal guardian of, from a bank or approved institution. There is no upper limit, but it is available for 8 years from the year you start repaying. Only interest qualifies, not principal.

question: How does 80C work?
answer: Section 80C lets you deduct up to ₹1.5 lakh a year of eligible investments and expenses from taxable income in the old regime. Eligible items include EPF and VPF, PPF, ELSS mutual funds (3-year lock-in), life-insurance premiums, 5-year tax-saver bank FDs, NSC, Sukanya Samriddhi, home-loan principal repayment, and tuition fees for up to two children. At the 30% slab, a full ₹1.5 lakh saves ₹46,800 of tax (including cess). It is not available in the new regime.

question: Which investments qualify for 80C?
answer: EPF/VPF, PPF, Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, NSC, 5-year tax-saver FD or post-office time deposit, ELSS mutual funds, life insurance premium (own, spouse, children), ULIPs, NPS Tier 1 (via 80CCD(1)), Senior Citizen Savings Scheme, home-loan principal, stamp duty on a house purchase, and tuition fees. The combined cap across 80C, 80CCC and 80CCD(1) is ₹1.5 lakh.

question: What is the lock-in for ELSS?
answer: Three years from the date of each investment — the shortest among 80C options (PPF is 15 years, tax-saver FD 5 years). For SIPs, each instalment has its own 3-year lock-in. After that, gains are long-term capital gains: 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh of equity LTCG a year.

question: What is section 80D?
answer: Deduction (old regime) for health-insurance premiums: up to ₹25,000 for yourself, spouse and children, plus another ₹25,000 for parents — ₹50,000 if they are senior citizens (and ₹50,000 for yourself if you are a senior). Up to ₹5,000 of preventive health check-ups fits inside these limits. Premiums must be paid by any mode other than cash.

question: Maximum 80D deduction for a family with senior-citizen parents?
answer: ₹75,000: ₹25,000 for your own family's policy plus ₹50,000 for senior-citizen parents. If you are also a senior citizen the total can reach ₹1 lakh. A senior parent with no insurance can claim actual medical expenses up to ₹50,000 instead.

question: What is 80CCD(1B)?
answer: An additional ₹50,000 deduction for your own contribution to NPS Tier 1, over and above the ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit — so old-regime taxpayers can deduct up to ₹2 lakh of NPS + 80C investments. At the 30% slab the extra ₹50,000 saves ₹15,600 of tax. It is not available in the new regime.

question: Is employer NPS contribution tax-free?
answer: Yes, under 80CCD(2): the employer's contribution to your NPS is deductible up to 14% of basic + DA (in the new regime and for government employees; 10% for private-sector employees in the old regime). This is one of the few deductions that survives in the new regime. Note the overall cap: employer EPF + NPS + superannuation above ₹7.5 lakh a year is taxable.

question: What is 80TTA?
answer: Deduction of up to ₹10,000 a year on interest from savings bank accounts (not FDs) for individuals below 60 in the old regime. Senior citizens instead get 80TTB: up to ₹50,000 on interest from savings accounts and fixed deposits.

question: Can I claim both 80C and 80CCD(1B) for NPS?
answer: Yes. Your own NPS contribution first counts under 80CCD(1) inside the ₹1.5 lakh 80C ceiling; any extra up to ₹50,000 goes under 80CCD(1B). Many people fill 80C with EPF/PPF/ELSS and use the ₹50,000 80CCD(1B) slot purely for NPS.

question: What is section 80G?
answer: Deduction for donations to approved charities and funds (old regime). Some funds like the PM National Relief Fund give 100% deduction; most registered NGOs give 50%, sometimes limited to 10% of your adjusted gross income. Cash donations above ₹2,000 do not qualify; the donee must file Form 10BD and give you a certificate (Form 10BE).

question: Do tuition fees qualify for 80C?
answer: Yes — tuition fees (not donations, development fees or transport) paid to any school, college or university in India for up to two children, inside the ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit. Both parents can claim separately for different children.

question: Does home-loan principal count under 80C?
answer: Yes, the principal portion of your home-loan EMIs (and stamp duty/registration charges in the year of purchase) is deductible under 80C within ₹1.5 lakh. The interest portion is claimed separately under 24(b) up to ₹2 lakh. If you sell the house within 5 years of possession the 80C claims are reversed.

question: What is Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana?
answer: A government small-savings scheme for a girl child under 10: deposit ₹250 to ₹1.5 lakh a year for 15 years, the account matures 21 years after opening (or on her marriage after 18). Interest is 8.2% a year (reviewed quarterly), and it is EEE — deposits under 80C, interest and maturity tax-free. ₹1.5 lakh a year for 15 years grows to roughly ₹72 lakh at 8.2%.
source: SSY rules; India Post / NSI rate table (8.2% for 2025-26)

question: What is NSC?
answer: National Savings Certificate: a 5-year post-office investment with a fixed rate (7.7% for 2025-26), compounded annually and paid at maturity. The investment qualifies for 80C, and the yearly accrued interest is deemed reinvested, so it also counts under 80C except in the final year. Interest is taxable at slab rates.
source: National Savings Certificate (VIII Issue) rules; NSI rate table

question: Is life-insurance premium deductible?
answer: Under 80C, yes (old regime), provided the premium is no more than 10% of the sum assured for policies issued after 1 April 2012. Maturity proceeds are tax-free under 10(10D) only if that 10% condition holds, and for policies issued after 1 April 2023 the aggregate annual premium must be ≤ ₹5 lakh (₹2.5 lakh for ULIPs).

question: What is section 80DDB?
answer: Deduction (old regime) for the cost of treating specified serious illnesses (cancer, chronic kidney failure, Parkinson's, etc.) of yourself or a dependant: up to ₹40,000, or ₹1 lakh for a senior citizen, reduced by any insurance reimbursement. You need a prescription from the relevant specialist.

question: What is a tax-saver FD?
answer: A 5-year fixed deposit with a bank or post office that qualifies for 80C (up to ₹1.5 lakh). No premature withdrawal or loan against it. Interest is fully taxable at your slab and TDS applies, so the post-tax return is lower than PPF or ELSS for 30%-slab taxpayers.

question: What is LTA and how is it exempt?
answer: Leave Travel Allowance covers the travel fare (not hotels or food) for you and your family on holiday within India. It is exempt under 10(5) for two journeys in a block of four calendar years (current block 2026–29), limited to economy air fare or AC first-class rail fare by the shortest route. Old regime only; you must submit tickets to your employer.

question: How does deduction for a disabled dependant work (80DD)?
answer: If you maintain a dependant with at least 40% disability you can deduct a flat ₹75,000 (₹1.25 lakh for severe, 80%+ disability) regardless of actual spending, with a medical certificate in Form 10-IA. Section 80U gives the same flat amounts to a taxpayer who is themselves disabled. Old regime only.

question: Can I claim a deduction for rent without HRA?
answer: Yes, section 80GG (old regime): if you do not receive HRA and do not own a house where you live, you can deduct the least of ₹5,000 a month, 25% of total income, or rent paid minus 10% of total income. File Form 10BA with the return.

question: What tax benefit does an electric-vehicle loan get?
answer: Section 80EEB allowed up to ₹1.5 lakh a year of interest on a loan for an electric vehicle, but only for loans sanctioned between 1 April 2019 and 31 March 2023. New loans get no such deduction; EVs still attract a lower GST of 5%.

question: What is the maximum tax I can save with all common old-regime deductions?
answer: A typical salaried stack: standard deduction ₹50,000, 80C ₹1.5 lakh, 80CCD(1B) ₹50,000, 80D ₹25,000 (₹75,000 with senior parents), 24(b) home-loan interest ₹2 lakh, plus HRA (varies). Excluding HRA that is about ₹5–5.5 lakh of deductions; at the 30% slab with cess, each ₹1 lakh of deduction saves ₹31,200.
source: Sum of section limits; 30% slab × 1.04 cess

question: Is EPF withdrawal taxable?
answer: Not if you have five years of continuous service (periods with previous employers count if the balance was transferred). Withdrawing earlier makes the employer's contribution and all interest taxable, reverses the 80C benefit on your own contributions, and attracts 10% TDS if the amount exceeds ₹50,000 (20% without PAN).
source: s.10(12), Rule 8 Part A Fourth Schedule; s.192A

question: Which ITR form should a salaried person use?
answer: ITR-1 (Sahaj) if you are a resident individual with total income up to ₹50 lakh from salary or pension, one house property, other sources (interest, dividends) and agricultural income up to ₹5,000; from AY 2025-26 it also allows long-term capital gains on listed equity up to ₹1.25 lakh. If you have more than one house, foreign assets, unlisted shares, capital gains beyond that, or you are a company director, use ITR-2.
source: ITR-1 eligibility notes, incometax.gov.in; CBDT notification for AY 2025-26 forms

question: ITR-1 vs ITR-2 — what is the difference?
answer: ITR-1 is the simple form for resident individuals with salary, one house property and other-source income up to ₹50 lakh. ITR-2 is for individuals and HUFs without business income who have anything more complex: capital gains (beyond the small LTCG allowed in ITR-1), more than one house property, foreign income or assets, income above ₹50 lakh, directorships, unlisted shares, or losses to carry forward.

question: Who should file ITR-3?
answer: Individuals and HUFs with income from a business or profession that is not under the presumptive schemes — including freelancers keeping books, partners in firms, and anyone with futures-and-options or intraday trading income (these count as business income). ITR-3 also covers salary, house property and capital gains alongside.

question: ITR-3 kiske liye hai?
answer: ITR-3 un individuals/HUF ke liye hai jinki income business ya profession se aati hai aur jo presumptive scheme (44AD/44ADA) nahi le rahe — jaise books rakhne wale freelancers, firm ke partners, aur F&O ya intraday traders (yeh business income maani jaati hai). Salary, house property aur capital gains bhi isi form mein report hote hain.

question: What is ITR-4 (Sugam)?
answer: ITR-4 is for resident individuals, HUFs and partnership firms (not LLPs) with total income up to ₹50 lakh who declare business or professional income on a presumptive basis: 44AD (small business, 8% of turnover or 6% for digital receipts), 44ADA (professionals, 50% of receipts) or 44AE (goods vehicles). From AY 2025-26 it also allows listed-equity LTCG up to ₹1.25 lakh.

question: Which ITR for salary plus capital gains from shares?
answer: ITR-2, unless the only capital gain is long-term gain on listed equity/equity funds of ₹1.25 lakh or less (then ITR-1 works from AY 2025-26). Any short-term capital gain, LTCG above ₹1.25 lakh, or losses to carry forward require ITR-2. If you also trade F&O or intraday, it becomes ITR-3.

question: Which ITR form should a freelancer use?
answer: ITR-4 if you opt for presumptive taxation under 44ADA (gross receipts up to ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh with ≤ 5% cash receipts; 50% of receipts deemed profit). If you want to deduct actual expenses or your receipts are higher, keep books and file ITR-3.

question: What is the due date for filing ITR?
answer: 31 July after the end of the financial year for individuals who do not need an audit (for AY 2025-26 the CBDT extended it to mid-September 2025); 31 October for audit cases. A belated or revised return can be filed until 31 December of the assessment year, with a late fee of ₹5,000 (₹1,000 if total income is up to ₹5 lakh) and loss of carry-forward of most losses.

question: Can I file a return after the deadline?
answer: Yes — a belated return under 139(4) until 31 December of the assessment year, with the 234F late fee (₹1,000 or ₹5,000) and interest under 234A on unpaid tax; business and capital losses cannot be carried forward. After that, an updated return (ITR-U) can be filed within 48 months of the end of the assessment year by paying 25% to 70% additional tax, but it cannot reduce tax or claim a refund.
source: ss.139(4), 139(8A), 234F; Finance Act 2025 extended ITR-U to 48 months

question: What is a revised return?
answer: If you discover a mistake after filing (missed income, wrong bank account, unclaimed deduction) you can file a revised return under 139(5) any number of times up to 31 December of the assessment year or before the assessment is completed. The revised return replaces the original.

question: Do I need to file a return if my income is below the taxable limit?
answer: Not mandatory below the basic exemption, but you must file if you deposited ₹1 crore+ in current accounts (₹50 lakh in savings), spent ₹2 lakh+ on foreign travel or ₹1 lakh+ on electricity, had TDS/TCS of ₹25,000+ (₹50,000 for seniors), have foreign assets, or want a refund or to carry forward losses. Filing also helps with loans and visas.

question: How do I e-verify my ITR?
answer: Within 30 days of filing: Aadhaar OTP, net-banking, bank-account or demat EVC, or a Digital Signature Certificate. Alternatively sign the ITR-V acknowledgement and post it to CPC Bengaluru. An unverified return is treated as not filed.

question: What happens if I don't file ITR at all?
answer: The department can issue notices, levy the 234F late fee, charge 234A interest, and in serious cases prosecute. You lose refunds of excess TDS, cannot carry forward losses, and face higher TDS/TCS rates as a 'non-filer' under 206AB. Loan and visa applications usually ask for the last 2–3 years of ITRs.

question: What is Form 10-IEA?
answer: The form a person with business or professional income files to opt out of the new tax regime (or to re-enter it, which is allowed only once). It must be filed before the ITR due date. Salaried people without business income do not need it — they just pick the regime in the ITR.

question: What is TDS mismatch and how do I fix it?
answer: If the TDS in your return does not match Form 26AS, CPC will reduce your credit. Fix it by asking the deductor (employer, bank) to revise their TDS return so the correct amount shows in 26AS, then file a rectification under 154 or a revised return. Always reconcile Form 16/16A with 26AS and AIS before filing.

question: How long does an income-tax refund take?
answer: Usually 2–6 weeks after e-verification once CPC processes the return, credited to a pre-validated bank account. Refunds earn 0.5% a month interest under 244A from 1 April (if the return was filed on time). Check status on the e-filing portal or NSDL's refund tracker.

question: What is the presumptive scheme under 44AD?
answer: Small businesses with turnover up to ₹2 crore (₹3 crore if cash receipts are ≤ 5%) can declare 8% of turnover (6% for digital receipts) as profit without maintaining books or getting audited. Once opted, you should stay in it for 5 years; opting out early forces books and audit for the next 5 years. Not available for commission agents or professionals.

question: When is a tax audit required?
answer: Under 44AB when business turnover exceeds ₹1 crore (₹10 crore if cash receipts and payments are each ≤ 5%), or professional receipts exceed ₹50 lakh, or when you declare profit below the presumptive rate while income exceeds the basic exemption. The audit report (Form 3CA/3CB-3CD) is due by 30 September; the ITR by 31 October.

question: Is F&O trading income business income?
answer: Yes — futures and options are treated as non-speculative business income, so you file ITR-3, can deduct expenses, and can carry forward losses for 8 years (set off against any business income). Intraday equity is speculative business (losses only against speculative gains, carried 4 years). Turnover for audit is computed from absolute profit and loss.
source: s.43(5) proviso; ICAI guidance note on tax audit

question: What is Form 15G / 15H?
answer: Self-declarations given to banks so that no TDS is deducted on interest when your total tax liability is nil: 15G for people under 60 (total income within the exemption limit and interest below it), 15H for senior citizens. Submit at the start of each financial year; the bank reports them to the department.

question: What are the consequences of a wrong HRA or 80C claim?
answer: If a claim cannot be backed by rent receipts, landlord PAN or investment proofs, the department can add the amount back, charge interest, and levy a penalty of 50% (under-reporting) or 200% (misreporting) of the tax evaded under 270A. The e-filing portal now cross-checks rent claims against the landlord's reported income.

question: Can I file ITR myself for free?
answer: Yes. The incometax.gov.in e-filing portal is free: log in with PAN, pick the form, use the pre-filled data from AIS/26AS, check and submit, then e-verify. Most salaried people with Form 16 can finish ITR-1 in under an hour. Paid tools and CAs help when you have capital gains, business income or foreign assets.

question: What is the difference between financial year and assessment year?
answer: The financial year (FY) is when you earn the income — 1 April to 31 March. The assessment year (AY) is the following year in which that income is assessed and the return is filed. Income earned in FY 2025-26 is reported in AY 2026-27.

question: Do I pay tax on gifts?
answer: Gifts above ₹50,000 in a year from non-relatives are taxed as 'income from other sources' at your slab (the whole amount, not just the excess). Gifts from relatives (spouse, parents, siblings, children, lineal ancestors/descendants and their spouses), at marriage, by will or inheritance are exempt. Cash gifts of ₹2 lakh or more are separately penalised under 269ST.

question: How is LTCG on equity taxed now?
answer: For listed shares and equity mutual funds held more than 12 months, long-term capital gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year are taxed at 12.5% (plus cess) since 23 July 2024; the first ₹1.25 lakh is exempt. Gains up to 31 January 2018 are grandfathered. Securities transaction tax must have been paid on the sale.
source: s.112A as amended by Finance (No. 2) Act 2024

question: What is STCG tax on shares?
answer: Short-term capital gains on listed shares and equity funds (held 12 months or less) are taxed at 20% plus cess since 23 July 2024 (15% before that). There is no exemption limit, but the gains can be set off against short-term or long-term capital losses.
source: s.111A as amended by Finance (No. 2) Act 2024

question: LTCG on ₹2 lakh gains in equity — how much tax?
answer: Only ₹75,000 is taxable (₹2,00,000 − ₹1,25,000 exemption). Tax = 12.5% of ₹75,000 = ₹9,375, plus 4% cess ₹375 = ₹9,750. If you also had long-term capital losses, they reduce the gain first.

question: How are debt mutual funds taxed?
answer: Debt funds bought on or after 1 April 2023 (equity ≤ 35%) are 'specified mutual funds': all gains are taxed at your slab rate whatever the holding period, with no indexation. Units bought before April 2023 and sold after 23 July 2024 get 12.5% without indexation if held over 24 months.

question: How is property capital gain taxed?
answer: A house sold after 24 months is long-term: 12.5% without indexation for sales from 23 July 2024; residents who bought before that date may instead pay 20% with indexation if it is lower. Short-term gains (≤ 24 months) are taxed at slab. You can save the tax by reinvesting in another house (section 54, up to ₹10 crore) or in 54EC bonds (₹50 lakh within 6 months).

question: What is indexation?
answer: Adjusting the purchase price for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index so that only real gains are taxed. Since 23 July 2024 indexation has largely been removed (flat 12.5% LTCG), surviving only as an option for land and buildings bought before that date by resident individuals and HUFs.
source: s.48 second proviso; CII notified yearly by CBDT

question: Can capital losses be carried forward?
answer: Yes, for 8 assessment years, provided you file the return by the due date. Short-term losses can offset short- or long-term gains; long-term losses only offset long-term gains. Losses cannot be set off against salary or other income.

question: How are crypto gains taxed in India?
answer: Virtual digital assets are taxed at a flat 30% plus cess on gains, with no deduction except the cost of acquisition, no set-off of losses against other income or other crypto, and 1% TDS on each transfer above ₹10,000 (₹50,000 for small taxpayers). Gifts of crypto are taxable for the receiver.

question: What is the tax on gold?
answer: Physical gold, gold ETFs and gold funds sold after 24 months are long-term: 12.5% without indexation (since July 2024); within 24 months, gains are added to income at slab rates. Sovereign Gold Bonds are tax-free if held to the 8-year maturity; interest of 2.5% a year is taxable. Buying gold above ₹2 lakh in cash is barred; 3% GST applies on purchase.

question: Is dividend income taxable?
answer: Yes, since FY 2020-21 dividends are taxed in your hands at slab rates under 'income from other sources'. Companies and mutual funds deduct 10% TDS once dividends exceed ₹10,000 in a year (threshold raised in Budget 2025). Interest on a loan taken to buy the shares is deductible up to 20% of the dividend.

question: How is an SIP taxed when I redeem?
answer: Each SIP instalment is a separate purchase, redeemed first-in-first-out. Units older than 12 months (equity) are long-term — 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption; younger units are short-term at 20%. Your fund house's capital gains statement does this FIFO calculation for you.

question: Does section 54 apply to a flat under construction?
answer: Yes — to claim 54 exemption you must buy a residential house within 1 year before or 2 years after the sale, or complete construction within 3 years. Money not used by the ITR due date must be parked in a Capital Gains Account Scheme deposit. The exemption is capped at ₹10 crore of gains.

question: What are the GST slabs?
answer: Since 22 September 2025 (the 'GST 2.0' rationalisation decided at the 56th GST Council meeting) India has two main rates: 5% for merit goods and services and 18% as the standard rate, plus a 40% rate for sin and luxury items (tobacco, pan masala, aerated drinks, large cars). Many essentials — UHT milk, paneer, Indian breads, life and health insurance — are exempt. Special rates remain for gold/silver (3%) and rough diamonds (0.25%). The old 12% and 28% slabs were removed.
source: GST Council 56th meeting recommendations (3 Sept 2025), effective 22 Sept 2025

question: How do GST input tax credits work?
answer: Input tax credit (ITC) lets a registered business subtract the GST it paid on purchases from the GST it collects on sales, so tax applies only on value added. Conditions (section 16): a valid tax invoice, goods or services actually received, the supplier has paid the tax and reported the invoice (it appears in your GSTR-2B), you file your return, and you pay the supplier within 180 days. Example: ₹18,000 output GST − ₹11,000 ITC = ₹7,000 payable.

question: Which ITC is blocked under GST?
answer: Section 17(5) blocks credit on motor vehicles with up to 13 seats (unless used for transport business, driving schools or resale), food and beverages, outdoor catering, club and gym memberships, personal consumption, goods lost or given as free samples, works-contract and construction of immovable property for own use, and anything used for exempt supplies.

question: Who must register for GST?
answer: Businesses with aggregate turnover above ₹40 lakh for goods (₹20 lakh for services; ₹20 lakh / ₹10 lakh in special category north-eastern and hill states). Registration is compulsory regardless of turnover for inter-state suppliers of goods, e-commerce sellers (with some relief for small intra-state sellers), casual taxable persons, those liable under reverse charge, and input service distributors.

question: What is the GST composition scheme?
answer: A simplified scheme for small businesses with turnover up to ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh in special-category states): pay a flat 1% of turnover (manufacturers and traders), 5% for restaurants, or 6% for service providers up to ₹50 lakh. You cannot collect GST from customers, cannot claim ITC, cannot sell inter-state, and file CMP-08 quarterly plus GSTR-4 annually.
source: CGST Act s.10; Notification 2/2019-CT (Rate) for services

question: What is the difference between CGST, SGST and IGST?
answer: On a sale within a state the GST is split equally into CGST (to the Centre) and SGST (to the state) — 18% becomes 9% + 9%. On an inter-state sale or import the whole 18% is charged as IGST, collected by the Centre and shared. ITC of IGST can be used against IGST, CGST and SGST, but CGST credit cannot be used for SGST or vice versa.

question: GST at 18% on ₹45,000 — what is the total?
answer: GST = 18% × ₹45,000 = ₹8,100 (₹4,050 CGST + ₹4,050 SGST within a state, or ₹8,100 IGST inter-state). Invoice total = ₹53,100. If a price is quoted GST-inclusive, the base is price ÷ 1.18: ₹53,100 ÷ 1.18 = ₹45,000.

question: What is reverse charge under GST?
answer: Normally the seller collects and pays GST; under reverse charge mechanism (RCM) the buyer pays it directly. It applies to notified cases such as goods transport agencies, legal services from advocates, sponsorship, security services from non-corporates, imported services, and some purchases from unregistered suppliers (e.g. by builders). RCM tax must be paid in cash and can then be claimed as ITC if eligible.

question: What is GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and GSTR-9?
answer: GSTR-1 reports your outward supplies invoice by invoice (monthly by the 11th, or quarterly under QRMP). GSTR-3B is the monthly summary return where you declare output tax, claim ITC and pay (by the 20th, or 22nd/24th for QRMP). GSTR-9 is the annual return due 31 December (GSTR-9C reconciliation if turnover exceeds ₹5 crore). GSTR-2B is the auto-drafted ITC statement you reconcile against.

question: What is e-invoicing and who needs it?
answer: Businesses with aggregate turnover above ₹5 crore (in any year since 2017-18) must report B2B invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an IRN and QR code; an invoice without it is invalid and the buyer cannot claim ITC. Invoices must be uploaded within 30 days for turnover above ₹10 crore.
source: Notification 10/2023-CT; GSTN advisory on the 30-day limit

question: What is an e-way bill?
answer: A document generated on the e-way bill portal before moving goods worth more than ₹50,000 (per invoice/consignment), containing the consignor, consignee, goods and vehicle details. Valid for 1 day per 200 km. Moving goods without it attracts a penalty of 200% of the tax or detention of the vehicle.

question: What is the GST rate on restaurant bills?
answer: 5% without input tax credit for standalone restaurants and food delivery (the delivery app collects it on restaurant orders); 18% with ITC in restaurants inside hotels with room tariff above ₹7,500. Service charge added by the restaurant is optional and not a tax.
source: Notification 11/2017-CT (Rate) as amended; CCPA guidelines on service charge

question: GST on restaurant bills?
answer: Most restaurant and food-delivery bills carry 5% GST (no input credit for the restaurant). Restaurants in hotels where rooms cost more than ₹7,500 a night charge 18%. Any 'service charge' is a restaurant tip, not GST, and can be refused.

question: Is GST charged on health insurance?
answer: Not any more for individuals: from 22 September 2025 premiums on individual life insurance (term, ULIP, endowment) and individual health insurance (including family floater and senior-citizen plans) are exempt from GST. Group policies bought by companies still attract 18%.
source: GST Council 56th meeting decision, effective 22 Sept 2025

question: What is GSTIN?
answer: A 15-character GST identification number: the first 2 digits are the state code, the next 10 are the PAN, the 13th is the entity number for that PAN in the state, the 14th is 'Z' by default and the 15th is a checksum. Always verify a supplier's GSTIN on the GST portal before claiming ITC.
source: GST registration rules; gst.gov.in search taxpayer

question: What is the penalty for late GST filing?
answer: Late fee of ₹50 a day (₹25 CGST + ₹25 SGST), or ₹20 a day for a nil return, capped per return based on turnover; plus interest at 18% a year on tax paid late (24% on wrongly claimed ITC). Non-filing for six months can lead to cancellation of registration, and GSTR-1 is blocked if GSTR-3B is pending.

question: Can a freelancer claim GST input credit on a laptop?
answer: Yes, if the freelancer is GST-registered and the laptop is used for the taxable business: the 18% GST on the invoice (which must carry your GSTIN) can be claimed as ITC against the GST you charge clients. If you also use it personally, claim proportionately. Composition dealers cannot claim ITC.

question: Is GST applicable on exports of services?
answer: Exports are zero-rated: you can export under a Letter of Undertaking without charging GST and claim a refund of the ITC on your inputs, or pay IGST and claim it back. A service counts as an export only if the recipient is outside India, payment arrives in convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits) and the place of supply is outside India.

question: What is the GST on a flat purchase?
answer: Under-construction homes: 5% without ITC (1% for affordable housing — up to ₹45 lakh and 60/90 sq m carpet area). Ready-to-move flats with a completion certificate, and resale flats, attract no GST (only stamp duty and registration).

question: Do I need GST registration to sell on Amazon or Flipkart?
answer: Generally yes for sellers of goods — marketplaces require a GSTIN and deduct 0.5% TCS. Since October 2023, small intra-state sellers below the threshold can sell without registration using an enrolment number, but they cannot sell across states.

question: What is TCS under GST for e-commerce?
answer: E-commerce operators collect tax at source at 0.5% (0.25% CGST + 0.25% SGST, reduced from 1% in July 2024) on the net value of sales made through their platform and deposit it in GSTR-8. The seller sees it in their electronic cash ledger and can use it to pay GST.
source: CGST Act s.52; Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 rate cut

question: What is HSN / SAC code?
answer: HSN (Harmonised System of Nomenclature) codes classify goods and SAC codes classify services for GST rates and reporting. Businesses with turnover up to ₹5 crore must show 4-digit HSN on B2B invoices; above ₹5 crore, 6 digits. The code decides which rate applies, so a wrong HSN can mean a wrong tax rate.

question: Is GST payable on a UPI payment or bank transfer?
answer: No — GST is on the supply of goods or services, not on the mode of payment. UPI transactions themselves are free for consumers. The invoice amount already includes any GST the seller charges; paying by UPI, card or cash does not change it.
source: GST levy is on supply (CGST Act s.9); NPCI UPI pricing

question: What is the GST rate on mobile phones and laptops?
answer: Since the September 2025 rate rationalisation, mobile phones stay at 18% and laptops/computers at 18%. Earlier phones were at 12% before 2020 and 18% since; TVs up to 32 inches moved to 18% and larger TVs dropped from 28% to 18% in 2025.
source: GST rate schedule as notified after the 56th Council meeting

question: What are the GST rates on cars?
answer: After 22 September 2025 small cars (petrol up to 1,200 cc / diesel up to 1,500 cc, under 4 m) are taxed at 18% (down from 28% plus cess); larger cars, SUVs and luxury vehicles are at the 40% rate with no separate cess. Electric vehicles remain at 5%.

question: What is GST on gold jewellery?
answer: 3% GST on the value of gold plus 5% GST on making charges (if billed separately). Buying gold worth ₹2 lakh or more in cash is prohibited under income-tax rules, and jewellers must note PAN for purchases above ₹2 lakh.
source: GST rate schedule (3% on gold); s.269ST

question: What is the time of supply under GST?
answer: The point when GST becomes payable. For goods it is the earlier of invoice date or delivery; for services the earlier of invoice (if issued within 30 days) or payment. Under reverse charge it is the earlier of payment or 60 days from invoice. This decides which month's GSTR-3B must include the tax.

question: What is a credit note under GST?
answer: A document a supplier issues to reduce the value or tax on an earlier invoice (returns, discounts, errors). It is reported in GSTR-1 and reduces output tax, provided the buyer reverses the matching ITC and it is issued by 30 November following the financial year.

question: What is the QRMP scheme?
answer: Quarterly Return, Monthly Payment: taxpayers with turnover up to ₹5 crore can file GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B quarterly while paying tax monthly through a challan (35% of the previous quarter's tax or self-assessed). The Invoice Furnishing Facility lets them upload B2B invoices monthly so buyers get ITC without delay.

question: Can I claim ITC on GST paid on office rent?
answer: Yes — rent for business premises is a taxable service at 18%, and a registered business can claim the ITC provided the landlord issues a proper tax invoice with your GSTIN and reports it. Residential property rented to a registered person for business falls under reverse charge, where you pay the GST and then claim it.
source: CGST Act s.16; Notification 05/2022-CT (Rate) on residential rent RCM

question: What is the GST refund process for excess ITC?
answer: Refunds arise mainly for exports/zero-rated supplies and inverted duty structure (inputs taxed higher than outputs). File RFD-01 within two years with invoices and a CA certificate above ₹2 lakh; 90% provisional refund for exporters within 7 days, final within 60 days, with interest at 6% if delayed.

question: Do small businesses below the GST threshold need to issue tax invoices?
answer: No — an unregistered business cannot charge or collect GST and simply issues a bill of supply/normal invoice. Charging GST without registration is an offence. Many small firms still register voluntarily to claim ITC and to work with corporate clients who require a GSTIN.

question: What is aggregate turnover for GST?
answer: The all-India total of taxable, exempt, export and inter-state supplies of all businesses under one PAN, excluding GST itself and inward supplies under reverse charge. It decides registration (₹40/20 lakh), the composition limit (₹1.5 crore), e-invoicing (₹5 crore) and annual-return thresholds.

question: What is TDS on FD interest?
answer: Banks deduct 10% TDS once the interest on all your deposits with that bank exceeds ₹50,000 in a financial year (₹1 lakh for senior citizens) — thresholds raised from ₹40,000/₹50,000 by Budget 2025. Without PAN the rate is 20%. The interest is still taxed at your slab; TDS is only an advance. Submit 15G/15H if your total income is below the taxable limit.
source: s.194A as amended by Finance Act 2025

question: What is TDS on FD?
answer: If a bank pays you more than ₹50,000 of interest in a year (₹1 lakh if you are a senior citizen) it deducts 10% as TDS and reports it in your 26AS. You then pay the balance tax at your slab (or claim a refund) when filing. Give Form 15G/15H to stop TDS if you have no tax liability.

question: What is TDS on rent?
answer: Individuals and HUFs paying more than ₹50,000 a month of rent must deduct 2% TDS under 194-IB (reduced from 5% in October 2024), once a year, and deposit it with Form 26QC. Businesses deduct 10% under 194-I once annual rent crosses ₹6 lakh (₹50,000 a month, raised in Budget 2025).

question: TDS on professional fees?
answer: Section 194J: 10% on fees for professional services (CA, lawyer, doctor, consultant) and 2% on technical services, call-centre work and royalties for films, once payments to one person exceed ₹50,000 in the year (raised from ₹30,000 in Budget 2025). Individuals not subject to tax audit do not need to deduct.

question: What is TDS on contractor payments?
answer: Section 194C: 1% if the contractor is an individual or HUF, 2% otherwise, on a single payment above ₹30,000 or annual payments above ₹1 lakh. Deposit by the 7th of the next month and file quarterly Form 26Q; the contractor gets Form 16A.

question: What is TCS on foreign remittance?
answer: Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme banks collect 20% TCS on remittances above ₹10 lakh a year (threshold raised from ₹7 lakh in Budget 2025) for investments, gifts and tour packages; education and medical remittances above ₹10 lakh attract 5%, and education funded by a bank loan attracts no TCS. TCS is credited in 26AS and adjustable against your tax.
source: s.206C(1G) as amended by Finance Act 2025

question: What is TDS on salary and how is it computed?
answer: Under 192 the employer estimates your annual tax (in the regime you declare), subtracts tax already deducted, and deducts the balance evenly from monthly salary. Declare investments and rent early in the year; proofs are collected around January–February, and any shortfall is recovered in the last months.
source: s.192; CBDT annual circular on salary TDS

question: What is Form 16A?
answer: The TDS certificate for non-salary payments — bank interest, professional fees, rent, commission — issued quarterly by the deductor from TRACES. Match it with Form 26AS before claiming the credit in your return.

question: What is the TDS rate without PAN?
answer: If you do not provide a PAN, TDS is deducted at the higher of the normal rate or 20% under section 206AA (5% for 194-O/194-Q cases), and you cannot claim the credit easily because it is not mapped to you. Always link PAN and Aadhaar — an inoperative PAN also triggers the 20% rate.
source: s.206AA; CBDT circular on inoperative PAN

question: Is TDS deducted on mutual fund redemptions?
answer: No TDS for resident investors on capital gains from mutual-fund redemptions; you pay the tax yourself. TDS of 10% applies only to dividend (IDCW) payouts above ₹10,000 a year under 194K. NRIs do face TDS on redemptions.

question: What is TDS on buying property?
answer: If you buy immovable property worth ₹50 lakh or more you must deduct 1% TDS from the seller's payment under 194-IA, deposit it through Form 26QB within 30 days of the month-end, and give the seller Form 16B. Agricultural land is exempt; NRI sellers fall under section 195 instead (higher rates, TAN needed).

question: What is TDS on cash withdrawals?
answer: Section 194N: banks deduct 2% TDS on cash withdrawals above ₹1 crore in a year from all accounts with that bank; for people who have not filed returns for 3 years the thresholds are ₹20 lakh (2%) and ₹1 crore (5%). It is adjustable against your tax.

question: What is TDS on online gaming winnings?
answer: Net winnings from online games are taxed at a flat 30% under 115BBJ and the platform deducts 30% TDS under 194BA at withdrawal or year-end, with no threshold. Lottery, crossword and TV-show winnings are also taxed at 30% with TDS above ₹10,000 per transaction.

question: What is the UPI transaction limit per day?
answer: For person-to-person payments NPCI caps a single UPI transaction at ₹1 lakh and most banks cap the day at ₹1 lakh (some allow only ₹5,000–25,000 in the first 24 hours after you register a new device). Verified merchant categories have higher caps — up to ₹2 lakh for several, and ₹5 lakh per transaction for hospitals, education, IPO applications, tax payments, insurance, capital-market and credit-card bill payments after NPCI's September 2025 revision (with daily caps of ₹6–10 lakh in those categories). Your bank or app may apply lower limits.
source: NPCI UPI limit circulars (incl. Sept 2025 P2M revision); bank-specific limits apply

question: UPI limit per day?
answer: Typically ₹1 lakh per day for sending money to people (₹1 lakh per transaction), set by NPCI and your bank; new devices are often restricted for the first 24 hours. Paying merchants in categories like hospitals, education, taxes, IPOs and insurance can go up to ₹5 lakh per transaction. Check your bank app for its own cap.
source: NPCI UPI limits; bank app settings

question: What is the UPI Lite limit?
answer: UPI Lite is an on-device wallet for small payments without a PIN: ₹1,000 per transaction and a wallet balance of up to ₹5,000 (raised by RBI in December 2024), with ₹5,000 of daily top-ups. UPI Lite X also works offline between two phones via NFC.
source: RBI circular Dec 2024 on UPI Lite; NPCI UPI Lite product note

question: What happens if a UPI payment fails but money is debited?
answer: Usually the bank reverses it automatically. RBI's turnaround-time rule says a failed UPI transaction where the beneficiary was not credited must be auto-reversed within one working day (T+1); if not, the bank owes you ₹100 per day of delay. Check the transaction status in your UPI app first (it can show 'pending' for up to 48 hours), then raise a dispute in the app or with your bank, and escalate to the RBI Ombudsman at cms.rbi.org.in if it is not resolved in 30 days.
source: RBI circular DPSS.CO.PD No.629 (19 Sept 2019) on TAT and compensation

question: Money debited but UPI failed, what now?
answer: Wait for the status to settle (many 'pending' payments complete or reverse within hours), then raise a complaint in the UPI app ('report an issue' on that transaction) quoting the UPI reference number. The bank must auto-reverse within T+1 working day or pay ₹100 per day compensation. If nothing happens in 30 days, complain to the RBI Integrated Ombudsman at cms.rbi.org.in.
source: RBI TAT harmonisation circular (2019); RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021

question: I sent money to the wrong UPI ID — can I get it back?
answer: A successful UPI payment cannot be reversed by the bank without the receiver's consent. Immediately contact your bank or the UPI app and ask them to request the receiver's bank; also call the NPCI/bank helpline. If the receiver refuses, you can complain to the RBI Ombudsman and file a police complaint, but recovery is not guaranteed — always verify the name shown before paying.

question: What is UPI AutoPay?
answer: A recurring e-mandate on UPI for subscriptions, SIPs, EMIs and bills. You approve the mandate once with your PIN; debits up to ₹15,000 then run without a PIN (₹1 lakh for mutual funds, insurance premiums and credit-card bills), with a pre-debit notification 24 hours earlier. You can pause or revoke the mandate in the app.
source: RBI e-mandate framework; NPCI UPI AutoPay limits

question: Is UPI free?
answer: Yes for customers — banks and apps cannot charge you for UPI payments from a bank account. Since April 2023 an interchange of up to 1.1% applies to merchant payments above ₹2,000 made from prepaid wallets, but it is paid by the merchant, not the payer.
source: NPCI circular on PPI interchange (March 2023); RBI/DoR zero-MDR policy

question: What is a UPI PIN and VPA?
answer: The Virtual Payment Address (VPA, e.g. name@bank) is the alias that hides your account number; the UPI PIN is the 4- or 6-digit secret you set with your debit card and use to authorise each payment. Never share the PIN — you only enter it to send money, never to receive it.
source: NPCI UPI product overview; RBI safety advisories

question: How do I link a credit card to UPI?
answer: RuPay credit cards can be linked in UPI apps (BHIM, PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm) to pay merchants by scanning QR codes; Visa/Mastercard credit cards are not supported for UPI except some bank-specific pilots. Merchant payments above ₹2,000 may carry a fee for the merchant; cash-back/reward rules follow the card.
source: NPCI RuPay credit card on UPI (2022)

question: What is UPI Circle?
answer: A delegated-payments feature where a primary user lets a trusted secondary user (child, parent, staff) make UPI payments from their account, either with full delegation (up to ₹15,000 a month, ₹5,000 per transaction) or with partial delegation where each payment needs the primary user's approval.

question: What should I do if I get a fraudulent UPI request?
answer: Decline it — you never need to enter your PIN to receive money. Report the ID in the app, and if you did lose money call the national cyber helpline 1930 or file on cybercrime.gov.in within the 'golden hour'; also inform your bank so the money can be frozen in the receiver's account. Banks must limit your liability if you report within 3 days.
source: RBI circular on limited customer liability (July 2017); MHA cyber helpline 1930

question: Why does my bank show a different UPI limit from my friend's?
answer: NPCI sets ceilings, but each bank sets its own per-transaction and daily limits within them (and lower limits for new devices, newly added accounts or high-risk patterns). Apps like Google Pay also apply their own caps (e.g. 20 transactions a day). Check 'UPI limits' in the app or your bank's FAQ.
source: NPCI UPI operating guidelines; bank limit pages

question: What is IMPS and its limit?
answer: Immediate Payment Service: instant 24×7 bank-to-bank transfer using account number + IFSC or mobile + MMID. NPCI allows up to ₹5 lakh per transaction; banks may charge ₹2.5–15 plus GST (free in many apps). Unlike UPI it does not need a VPA.
source: NPCI IMPS product page (limit raised to ₹5 lakh in 2014)

question: NEFT vs RTGS — what is the difference?
answer: NEFT settles in half-hourly batches, 24×7, with no minimum or maximum (banks may cap online transfers), and is free for online transactions. RTGS is real-time, 24×7, for amounts of ₹2 lakh and above, with no upper limit, usually used for large payments like property deals. Both need the beneficiary's account number and IFSC.

question: What is the time limit for a bank to resolve a failed card/ATM transaction?
answer: For ATM cash-not-dispensed cases the bank must reverse within 5 days (T+5) or pay ₹100 a day; for failed card payments at merchants (money debited, merchant not paid) auto-reversal is within T+5 days; for failed UPI/IMPS T+1. These timelines and the ₹100/day compensation come from RBI's 2019 turnaround-time circular.

question: What is the daily limit for mobile banking NEFT transfers?
answer: RBI sets no NEFT limit, but banks set their own daily online caps (often ₹10–25 lakh for retail net banking, lower in apps and for newly added beneficiaries — for example ₹50,000 in the first 24 hours). Visit a branch or raise the limit in net banking for larger transfers.
source: RBI NEFT FAQ; bank-specific limit policies

question: Can I pay income tax or GST through UPI?
answer: Yes. The income-tax e-filing portal's e-Pay Tax accepts UPI (and net banking, cards, RTGS/NEFT); UPI tax payments enjoy a higher cap (₹5 lakh per transaction). GST challans can be paid via UPI through the GST portal's e-payment options depending on the bank.
source: incometax.gov.in e-Pay Tax; NPCI UPI category limits

question: What is the UPI chargeback or dispute process for a merchant payment?
answer: If you paid but did not receive goods/services, first contact the merchant; then raise a dispute in the UPI app on that transaction (within 30 days ideally). The payer bank raises a chargeback through NPCI's dispute system; the merchant's bank must respond in the set timelines. Unresolved cases go to the RBI Ombudsman.
source: NPCI UPI dispute resolution (URCS); RBI Ombudsman

question: What is 'UPI number'?
answer: A UPI number is a numeric alias (your mobile number or a 8–9 digit number you choose) mapped to your VPA so people can pay you without typing an ID, and it works across apps. You can create it in the UPI app profile and link it to the bank account you prefer.

question: How does EPF work?
answer: Employees' Provident Fund is mandatory for establishments with 20+ employees (and for wages up to ₹15,000; above that it is optional but almost universal). You contribute 12% of basic + DA and your employer matches 12% — of which 8.33% (capped at ₹1,250 a month) goes to the Employees' Pension Scheme and 3.67% to your EPF account. EPFO credits interest yearly (8.25% for FY 2024-25). Your contribution qualifies for 80C; interest and withdrawal after 5 years are tax-free.
source: EPF & MP Act 1952; EPFO interest-rate notification (8.25% for 2024-25)

question: EPF interest rate and how it's credited
answer: EPFO announces the rate each year (8.25% for FY 2024-25, the same as the previous year) after the Finance Ministry approves it. Interest is computed monthly on the running balance but credited once a year, usually a few months after the year ends, which is why your passbook shows interest late. Interest on your own contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year is taxable.
source: EPFO circulars; s.10(11) proviso (₹2.5 lakh rule, Finance Act 2021)

question: How is EPF interest calculated?
answer: Interest is calculated on the monthly running balance: each month's closing balance × (annual rate ÷ 12). Example at 8.25%: a balance of ₹2,00,000 earns about ₹1,375 that month. Contributions made during the month earn interest from the next month. The total is credited to the account at year end.
source: EPFO interest computation rules (Para 60, EPF Scheme 1952)

question: What is UAN?
answer: The Universal Account Number is a 12-digit ID EPFO gives every member; it stays the same across employers and links all your PF member IDs. Activate it on the EPFO portal with Aadhaar, mobile and bank KYC to view the passbook, transfer balances when you change jobs, and file online withdrawal claims.

question: When can I withdraw my EPF fully?
answer: At retirement (58), or after two months of continuous unemployment, or on moving abroad permanently. You can take 75% of the balance after one month of unemployment and the rest after two. Withdrawing before 5 years of total service makes it taxable (10% TDS above ₹50,000). Transferring the balance to the new employer keeps the tax benefit and the service continuity.

question: Can I withdraw EPF partially for a house or medical emergency?
answer: Yes, EPFO allows advances: up to 36 months' basic + DA (or 90% of balance) for buying/constructing a house after 5 years of membership; 6 months' basic or the full employee share for medical treatment (no service minimum); 50% of your share for marriage or education after 7 years. Advances are not loans — nothing is repaid, and they are tax-free.

question: What is VPF?
answer: Voluntary Provident Fund: contributing more than the mandatory 12% (up to 100% of basic + DA) into your EPF account. It earns the same EPF interest (8.25%), qualifies for 80C, and the employer does not match it. Interest on your own contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year (EPF + VPF) is taxable.
source: EPF Scheme 1952 Para 26(6); Finance Act 2021 ₹2.5 lakh rule

question: What is EPS pension and how much will I get?
answer: The Employees' Pension Scheme is funded by the employer's 8.33% (on wages up to ₹15,000). After 10 years of service you get a monthly pension from 58: pensionable salary × pensionable service ÷ 70. With the ₹15,000 wage cap and 35 years' service the maximum is ₹7,500 a month; early pension from 50 is reduced 4% a year. Members with less than 10 years can withdraw the EPS amount instead.

question: What is EDLI?
answer: Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance comes free with EPF: if a member dies in service, the nominee gets a lump sum of up to ₹7 lakh (minimum ₹2.5 lakh after one year of continuous service), funded by the employer's 0.5% contribution. No separate enrolment is needed.
source: EDLI Scheme 1976 (benefit raised to ₹7 lakh in 2021)

question: How do I transfer EPF when I change jobs?
answer: Give your UAN to the new employer; then file Form 13 online on the EPFO member portal ('One Member – One EPF Account'). Since 2025 most transfers are auto-processed without employer attestation. Transferring keeps your service continuous (important for the 5-year tax-free rule and EPS pension).
source: EPFO Form 13 online transfer; EPFO circulars 2025

question: What is PPF and who can open it?
answer: Public Provident Fund is a 15-year government-backed savings scheme at a bank or post office. Any resident individual can open one (also for a minor child); HUFs and NRIs cannot open new accounts. Deposit ₹500 to ₹1.5 lakh a year in up to 12 instalments. It is EEE: deposits qualify for 80C, and interest and maturity are tax-free.

question: What is the PPF interest rate?
answer: 7.1% a year, compounded annually and credited on 31 March — unchanged since April 2020 (the government reviews small-savings rates every quarter). Interest for a month is computed on the lowest balance between the 5th and the end of the month, so deposit before the 5th to earn that month's interest.
source: Ministry of Finance quarterly small-savings rate notifications; PPF Scheme 2019 Para 5

question: PPF maturity rules
answer: PPF matures 15 financial years after the year of opening. You can withdraw the whole balance tax-free, extend without deposits (keep earning interest, one withdrawal a year), or extend with deposits in 5-year blocks (apply within a year of maturity; withdrawals limited to 60% of the balance at the start of the block).

question: How much will PPF of ₹1.5 lakh a year become in 15 years?
answer: At 7.1% with the deposit made at the start of each year, 15 deposits of ₹1.5 lakh (₹22.5 lakh invested) grow to about ₹40.7 lakh, all tax-free. ₹1 lakh a year gives about ₹27.1 lakh and ₹50,000 a year about ₹13.6 lakh. Extending for 5 more years at ₹1.5 lakh takes the corpus to roughly ₹66.6 lakh.

question: Can I withdraw from PPF before 15 years?
answer: Partial withdrawal is allowed from the 7th financial year: up to 50% of the balance at the end of the 4th year preceding the withdrawal year or the previous year, whichever is lower, once a year. Premature closure after 5 years is allowed only for serious illness, higher education or change of residency status, with a 1% interest penalty. A loan is available in years 3–6 at 1% interest.

question: PPF vs NPS — which is better?
answer: PPF is a guaranteed 7.1% tax-free debt product with a 15-year lock-in and a ₹1.5 lakh cap — safe but inflation-tight. NPS invests in equity and bonds (historically 9–12% long-term in equity-heavy choices), has an extra ₹50,000 80CCD(1B) deduction in the old regime and employer benefits in both regimes, but locks money till 60 and forces 40% into an annuity that is taxable. Many people use PPF for the safe part and NPS for the growth part of retirement savings.
source: PFRDA NPS returns history; PPF Scheme rules

question: What is NPS?
answer: The National Pension System is a PFRDA-regulated retirement account open to all Indian citizens aged 18–70. You invest regularly in a mix of equity (E), corporate bonds (C), government bonds (G) and alternatives (A) via pension fund managers at very low cost. At 60 you take up to 60% tax-free as a lump sum and use at least 40% to buy an annuity. Tax breaks: 80CCD(1), extra ₹50,000 under 80CCD(1B), and the employer's contribution under 80CCD(2).

question: NPS tax benefit under 80CCD(1B)
answer: Your own contribution to NPS Tier I gets an extra deduction of up to ₹50,000 under 80CCD(1B), on top of the ₹1.5 lakh 80C/80CCD(1) limit — available only in the old regime. At the 30% slab that is a saving of ₹15,600 a year. Tier II contributions get no deduction (except for central-government employees).

question: What is NPS Tier 1 vs Tier 2?
answer: Tier I is the pension account: tax benefits, locked until 60 (limited partial withdrawals), mandatory annuity at exit. Tier II is an optional savings account on top of an active Tier I: no lock-in, withdraw any time, same fund choices and low costs, but no tax deduction and gains are taxed like any investment.

question: How is NPS taxed at withdrawal?
answer: At 60, up to 60% of the corpus withdrawn as a lump sum is tax-free; at least 40% must buy an annuity, and the annuity income is taxed at slab rates each year. Partial withdrawals (up to 25% of your own contributions, max three times after three years) are tax-free. If the corpus is ₹5 lakh or less you can withdraw all of it.

question: What is the equity limit in NPS?
answer: Under Active Choice you can put up to 75% in equity (Scheme E) until age 50, tapering to 50% by 60; alternatives (A) are capped at 5%. Auto Choice lifecycle funds (Aggressive LC75, Moderate LC50, Conservative LC25) reduce equity automatically as you age.
source: PFRDA investment guidelines for NPS subscribers

question: Can I exit NPS before 60?
answer: Yes, after 5 years (3 years for those who joined after 60): you must put at least 80% into an annuity and can take 20% as lump sum — unless the corpus is ₹2.5 lakh or less, in which case the whole amount can be withdrawn. Partial withdrawals for specific needs (education, marriage, house, illness) are allowed from year three.

question: What is the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS)?
answer: An option under NPS for central-government employees from 1 April 2025: after 25 years of service it guarantees a pension of 50% of the average basic pay of the last 12 months (proportionate for 10–25 years, minimum ₹10,000 a month), with inflation indexation and 60% family pension. Employees contribute 10%; the government 18.5%.

question: What is NPS Vatsalya?
answer: An NPS account for minors launched in September 2024: parents or guardians invest at least ₹1,000 a year in the child's name; at 18 it converts to a regular NPS Tier I account. Budget 2025 extended the 80CCD(1B) ₹50,000 deduction (old regime) to contributions in a child's Vatsalya account.
source: PFRDA NPS Vatsalya scheme; Finance Act 2025

question: Is EPF or NPS mandatory?
answer: EPF is mandatory for eligible employees in covered establishments (and voluntary above the ₹15,000 wage threshold if you opted in at joining). NPS is mandatory only for central-government employees who joined after 1 January 2004 (and many state employees); for everyone else it is voluntary.

question: What is gratuity and how is it calculated?
answer: Gratuity is a lump sum an employer pays after at least 5 years of continuous service (also on death/disability): 15 days' last-drawn basic + DA for every completed year, i.e. (basic + DA) × 15/26 × years. Example: ₹50,000 and 10 years → ₹50,000 × 15/26 × 10 ≈ ₹2,88,462. Tax-free up to ₹20 lakh.

question: What is the Senior Citizen Savings Scheme?
answer: A post-office/bank scheme for residents aged 60+ (55+ for some retirees): deposit up to ₹30 lakh for 5 years (extendable 3 years) at 8.2% a year, paid quarterly. The deposit qualifies for 80C; interest is taxable, with TDS above ₹1 lakh (80TTB gives ₹50,000 deduction).

question: What is the Atal Pension Yojana?
answer: A government pension scheme for 18–40-year-olds (not income-tax payers, since Oct 2022): contribute a fixed monthly amount based on age and the pension you choose (₹1,000 to ₹5,000 a month from 60), with the spouse getting the same pension and the nominee the corpus. Contributions qualify under 80CCD(1).

question: How is a credit score calculated?
answer: Bureaus (CIBIL, Experian, Equifax, CRIF High Mark) score you from 300 to 900 using your credit history: payment history (roughly 35% weight — any late EMI or card payment hurts most), credit utilisation (about 30% — keep card balances under 30% of the limit), length of history (15%), credit mix of secured and unsecured loans (10%) and recent hard enquiries (10%). No loans or cards means no score ('NA/NH'), not a bad one.
source: TransUnion CIBIL methodology notes; RBI credit information regulations

question: Is 750 a good credit score?
answer: Yes — 750 and above is what most banks treat as 'good': you qualify for most loans and cards and often get the best rates. 650–749 is fair (loans possible, maybe higher rates); below 650 lenders become cautious. Scores above 800 are excellent.

question: What is CIBIL?
answer: TransUnion CIBIL is India's oldest credit bureau; 'CIBIL score' is its 3-digit score (300–900) summarising your loan and card repayment behaviour reported by lenders. Three other RBI-licensed bureaus — Experian, Equifax and CRIF High Mark — produce their own scores, which can differ slightly because lenders report to each separately.

question: How can I check my credit score for free?
answer: Every bureau must give you one free full credit report a year — use the CIBIL, Experian, Equifax and CRIF websites. Many apps (banks, Paytm, Google Pay, Paisabazaar) show free scores monthly; checking your own score is a soft enquiry and does not lower it.
source: RBI circular on free annual credit report (2016)

question: How do I improve my credit score?
answer: Pay every EMI and card bill in full and on time (set auto-pay), keep card utilisation below 30%, do not apply for many loans at once, keep old cards open to lengthen history, avoid settling loans for less than owed, and check your report for errors. Improvement usually shows within 3–6 months; bureaus now receive updates from lenders every fortnight.
source: RBI directive on fortnightly reporting (effective Jan 2025); CIBIL guidance

question: Does checking my own credit score reduce it?
answer: No. Checking your own score is a 'soft enquiry' and never affects it. Only 'hard enquiries' — when a lender pulls your report because you applied for credit — are recorded and can shave a few points if there are many in a short time.

question: How long do defaults stay on a credit report?
answer: Repayment history, including late payments and defaults, stays on your report for up to 7 years from the date of the event. A loan 'settled' for less than the full amount is flagged as 'settled' and hurts for years; paying the full amount and getting it marked 'closed' is far better.

question: What is credit utilisation ratio?
answer: The share of your total credit-card limit you are using: ₹30,000 outstanding on a ₹1 lakh limit is 30%. Lenders prefer below 30%; above 50% signals stress and drags the score down even if you pay in full. Asking for a higher limit or splitting spend across cards reduces the ratio.

question: Will closing a credit card improve my score?
answer: Usually the opposite: closing a card cuts your total limit (raising utilisation) and may shorten your credit history. Keep old, no-fee cards open with occasional small use; close a card only if it has a high annual fee or you cannot control spending.

question: What is a hard enquiry?
answer: A lender's check of your credit report when you apply for a loan or card. Each one is listed and too many in a short period (say 4–5 in a few months) lowers your score because it looks like credit hunger. Shop for loans within a short window and avoid applying to many lenders at once.

question: How can a student or first-job person build a credit score?
answer: Start with a secured credit card against a fixed deposit (₹10,000+), use it for small spends and pay in full every month; or take a small consumer-durable EMI and repay on time. In 6–12 months you will have a score. Being an authorised user on a parent's card also helps. Avoid instant BNPL apps piling up enquiries.

question: What if there is an error in my credit report?
answer: Raise a dispute online with the bureau; it must respond within 30 days after checking with the lender. Under RBI's October 2023 directions, credit institutions and bureaus that fail to resolve a complaint within 30 days must pay you ₹100 per day of delay. Keep loan closure letters and NOCs to prove your case.
source: RBI circular on strengthening customer service by CICs (Oct 2023)

question: Do EMI delays of a few days affect the credit score?
answer: Lenders generally report the days-past-due status at month end; a payment a few days late that is cleared within the same cycle often is not reported, but anything 30+ days past due certainly is and stays for years. Late fees and penal charges apply regardless, so always pay by the due date.

question: What is a credit card minimum amount due?
answer: Usually 5% of the outstanding balance (plus any EMIs and over-limit amounts). Paying only the minimum keeps the card active but the rest attracts 3–3.75% interest a month (36–45% a year) and you lose the interest-free period on new purchases. Always try to pay the total amount due.
source: Card issuer terms; RBI credit-card directions 2022

question: How does the credit card interest-free period work?
answer: Purchases made during a billing cycle are interest-free until the payment due date — typically 20 to 50 days depending on when in the cycle you buy — provided you pay the full statement amount. If you carry any balance, interest is charged from the transaction date on all purchases. Cash withdrawals never get a free period.
source: RBI Master Direction on credit and debit cards (2022)

question: What is the real cost of revolving ₹50,000 on a credit card?
answer: At 3.5% a month, carrying ₹50,000 for a year costs about ₹25,500 in interest (compounded monthly ≈ 51% effective), plus GST at 18% on the interest. A personal loan at 14% would cost about ₹7,000 for the same year — so converting card debt to EMIs or a loan is almost always cheaper.

question: What is a credit card billing cycle?
answer: The roughly 30-day period over which spends are collected into one statement; the due date falls about 15–25 days after the statement date. Buying right after the statement date gives you the longest interest-free stretch (up to ~50 days). RBI lets you change the cycle once to suit your salary date.
source: RBI Master Direction on credit cards (2022)

question: Does a co-applicant's score matter for a loan?
answer: Yes — banks check both applicants, and the weaker score can lead to a higher rate or rejection. A co-applicant with a good score and income helps you qualify for a bigger loan, but both are equally liable and the loan appears on both credit reports.

question: What is a 'no-cost EMI'?
answer: The retailer or brand pays the interest (as a discount to the bank), so you pay the price in equal instalments. There is still interest on the bank's books — the product discount is simply adjusted — and GST applies on that interest; some cards also charge a processing fee. Check that the total paid equals the sticker price.
source: RBI circular on zero-percent EMI schemes (2013); card issuer terms

question: What is BNPL and how does it affect credit?
answer: Buy-now-pay-later lets you defer small purchases for 15–45 days or convert them to EMIs through an NBFC partner. Most BNPL lines are reported to bureaus as loans, so missed repayments damage your score; many small open lines can also lower it. Use at most one and clear it on time.
source: RBI digital lending guidelines 2022; bureau reporting

question: How is EMI calculated?
answer: EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where P is the principal, r the monthly rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100) and n the number of months. Example: ₹10 lakh at 9% for 5 years → r = 0.0075, n = 60 → EMI ≈ ₹20,758; total paid ₹12.46 lakh, interest ₹2.46 lakh. Early EMIs are mostly interest; later ones mostly principal.
source: Standard amortisation formula (used by the app's emi tool)

question: EMI on 10 lakh at 9% for 5 years
answer: About ₹20,758 a month. Total repayment ₹12,45,501 over 60 months, of which ₹2,45,501 is interest. (Monthly rate 0.75%, n = 60.)

question: EMI for 25 lakh home loan at 8.5% for 20 years
answer: ₹21,696 a month. Over 240 months you repay ₹52.07 lakh, i.e. ₹27.07 lakh of interest on the ₹25 lakh borrowed. Shorter tenures cost less overall: 15 years → EMI ₹24,618 (interest ₹19.3 lakh); 10 years → ₹30,996 (interest ₹12.2 lakh).

question: EMI on 50 lakh at 8% for 20 years?
answer: ₹41,822 a month; total repayment about ₹1.0 crore, so interest of roughly ₹50.4 lakh over 20 years. Each 0.25% change in rate moves this EMI by about ₹800.

question: EMI on 5 lakh personal loan at 11% for 3 years
answer: ₹16,369 a month; total ₹5,89,297, interest ₹89,297. Add the processing fee (usually 1–2% + GST) to compare offers.

question: EMI on 3 lakh at 14% for 3 years
answer: ₹10,253 a month; total repayment ₹3,69,118, of which ₹69,118 is interest.

question: Car loan of 8 lakh at 10% for 7 years — EMI?
answer: ₹13,281 a month. Total paid ₹11.16 lakh, so interest of ₹3.16 lakh. A 5-year tenure would raise the EMI to about ₹17,000 but cut interest to roughly ₹2.2 lakh.

question: EMI on 2 lakh bike loan at 11% for 3 years
answer: ₹6,548 a month; you repay ₹2,35,719 in total, ₹35,719 of it interest.

question: EMI on 30 lakh at 9% for 15 years
answer: ₹30,428 a month; total repayment ₹54.77 lakh, interest ₹24.77 lakh.

question: EMI for 40 lakh home loan at 8.75% for 25 years
answer: ₹32,886 a month. Over 300 months you pay about ₹98.66 lakh — ₹58.66 lakh of interest, more than the loan itself, which is why prepaying a long loan early saves so much.

question: How does the tenure change my EMI and total interest?
answer: On ₹25 lakh at 8.5%: 10 years → EMI ₹30,996, interest ₹12.2 lakh; 15 years → ₹24,618, interest ₹19.3 lakh; 20 years → ₹21,696, interest ₹27.1 lakh. A longer tenure lowers the EMI but roughly doubles the interest. Pick the shortest tenure whose EMI stays under about 40% of take-home pay.

question: How much does the interest rate matter on a 25 lakh, 20-year loan?
